piezas.titulo: Rhythmic auditory stimulation combined with split-belt treadmill training improves spatiotemporal gait parameters in hemiparetic stroke patients: a randomized controlled trial
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundSplit-belt walking training (SWT) primarily ameliorates spatial gait asymmetry after stroke, yet its effect on temporal gait parameters remains limited. Rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) enhances cadence and rhythmicity via auditory–motor coupling. This study examined whether combining RAS with SWT yields greater walking benefits than SWT alone or conventional rehabilitation.MethodsThirty patients with post-stroke hemiparesis were randomized to RAS+SWT (n = 11), SWT alone (n = 8), or conventional rehabilitation (control, n = 11). Interventions were delivered for three weeks (five sessions/week). Primary outcomes were spatiotemporal gait parameters: walking speed, cadence, step length, and limping index. Linear mixed-effects models were used, with Hedges’ g for effect sizes.ResultsNo dropouts occurred. Significant time-group interactions were found for walking speed (F = 10.68, p < 0.001), cadence (F = 5.01, p = 0.014), and affected-side step length (F = 6.21, p = 0.006). The RAS+SWT group showed greater improvements than controls in walking speed (mean difference = 0.167, 95% CI [0.090, 0.245]), cadence (mean difference = 9.340, 95% CI [4.456, 14.223]), and step length (unaffected: mean difference = 0.077, 95% CI [0.039, 0.116]; affected: mean difference = 0.081, 95% CI [0.035, 0.127]), and greater walking speed improvements than the SWT group (mean difference = 0.110, 95% CI [0.022, 0.197]). For the limping index, a significant main effect of group was observed (F = 5.41, p = 0.011); however, the time-by-group interaction was not significant (F = 0.430, p = 0.655).ConclusionRAS combined with SWT is more effective than conventional rehabilitation in improving multidimensional spatiotemporal gait parameters—including walking speed, cadence, and affected-side step length—in patients with post-stroke hemiparesis. Compared with SWT alone, the combined intervention yielded greater improvements in walking speed, while no significant between-group differences were observed for cadence or step length. The combined protocol is feasible and safe.Clinical trial registrationChiCTR2600121963.

piezas.titulo: A Control-Theoretic Account of Cognitive Effort in Working Memory
piezas.resumenOriginal: Cognitive effort is closely linked to prefrontal control, but the control demands imposed by working memory remain poorly understood at the level of neural circuits. We formulated frontoparietal regulation as a feedback-control problem in a conductance-based spiking network comprising an intraparietal ring attractor and a recurrent dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) actuator. A local data-driven task-actuator model was identified around the cue-offset mnemonic state and used to design linear-quadratic regulation. Increasing memory load produced a strong monotonic rise in realized post-cue control effort, driven primarily by sustained dlPFC recruitment. Cue-aligned selective routing supported higher mnemonic loads with substantially less control effort than spatially nonspecific routing. Mean-matched open-loop stimulation reproduced much of the nominal retention benefit, whereas state-dependent feedback provided greater robustness when mnemonic activity was perturbed. Finite-horizon analysis revealed a strongly anisotropic, effectively low-dimensional control geometry dominated by a common mnemonic direction, with much weaker access to item-differentiating directions. These results link increasing working-memory demand to greater sustained prefrontal control requirements and show how frontoparietal routing geometry shapes the efficiency and robustness of mnemonic regulation.

Esto sugiere que la arquitectura de rutas frontoparietales podría usarse para diseñar intervenciones que reduzcan el gasto cognitivo.

piezas.titulo: Participation in Personal and Professional Roles After Young Adult Stroke: A Scoping Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceYoung adulthood is characterized by role developmental and occupational transitions; however, rehabilitation for young adult stroke survivors (YASS) is largely informed by evidence from older adults. Understanding the unique participation challenges of YASS is important for identifying tailored intervention targets.ObjectiveTo systematically map, synthesize, and identify gaps in the literature examining YASS participation.Data SourcesEBSCO search across Academic Search Ultimate, CINAHL Plus with Full Text, MEDLINE, and APA PsycInfo.Study Selection and Data CollectionPeer-reviewed studies reporting original data from YASS aged 18-45 that address participation in a role (e.g., parent, spouse), activity (e.g., education), or set of activities (e.g., activities of daily living). Data were extracted and synthesized to describe poststroke participation.FindingsFifteen studies reflected a heterogeneous evidence base. Findings suggest that stroke leads to occupational disruption with multi-layered and compounding effects on roles and activities during young adulthood.Conclusions and RelevanceStroke disrupts the life course trajectory through which roles, identities, future possibilities, and life structures are formed, negotiated, and adjusted.This review charted the limited and fragmented literature, indicating a need for evidence to inform clinical practices tailored to the distinct and evolving needs of YASS.
